subject: inconsistent CFA fit statistics--how to interpret

messages.author: b23e30760d1bfcd7
messages.subject: inconsistent CFA fit statistics--how to interpret
parts:
Hi all,

I ran a CFA model with 8 factors and 42 items on a large sample size of approximately 6000.  Because it's a likert scale measure, I chose WSLMV as the estimator for my CFA. 

What's interesting about the results is that while RMSEA (.05) and SRMR (.05) were within the acceptable range of <.08, the chi square of the model was significant (p <.001) and CFI and TLI were around .70, which is too low for acceptable model fit. 

Question 1:  Can someone kindly explain why this is the case (i.e, why CFI and TLI were not in the acceptable range but RMSEA and SRMR were)?  Overall, wouldn't you still conclude that there's still model misspecification, as not all the fit indices were in the acceptable range?

Also, my understanding is that if a chi square is signficiant, RMSEA should also be high, but that's not the case here. 

Question 2 + 3: what should I do to improve CFI and TLI? 


Thank you for your assistance!

Anh

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: inconsistent CFA fit statistics--how to interpret
parts: Can someone kindly explain why this is the case (i.e, why CFI and TLI were not in the acceptable range but RMSEA and SRMR were)?  Overall, wouldn't you still conclude that there's still model misspecification, as not all the fit indices were in the acceptable range?

Chi-squared is all that you need to tell you there is model misspecification.  Fit indices express the misspecification in different ways, to help assess the practical (not statistical) significance of the misspecification.  If incremental fit indices are low even other absolute fit measures are acceptable, I would guess your baseline model does not fit poorly enough for CFI/TLI to be useful.  Read the reference on the ?nullRMSEA help page in the semTools package.
Also, my understanding is that if a chi square is signficiant, RMSEA should also be high, but that's not the case here.

You misunderstand RMSEA.  Your model has many df across which to average out the misfit (not that this is necessarily a useful way to assess your model).  

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: d48f77c594fc7a99
messages.subject: Re: inconsistent CFA fit statistics--how to interpret
parts: Actually, there is an article answers your question, The Problem with Having Two Watches: Assessment of Fit When RMSEA and CFI Disagree. Basically, the author derived the sufficient and necessary conditions for the population inconsistency between CFI and RMSEA, the sample level inconsistency was evaluated as well. Though this article is supposed to be esoteric, it might be helpful to empirical researchers as well.
